data.title: Sotomayor suggests Supreme Court colleagues may applaud midterm results as safeguard
data.description:
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor on Friday suggested her colleagues may view Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections as a sign that their recent immunity decision has not eliminated checks on the president.

Speaking in Philadelphia, the liberal justice replied “absolutely” when asked if her colleagues were counting on elections as an institutional safeguard when issuing their landmark ruling granting Trump and former presidents broad criminal immunity.

“My colleagues today would probably applaud the last election, because they believe that if the people don’t like what’s happening, they can speak with their vote. And they did speak,” Sotomayor said.

“Now, they may not have liked the message — but I don’t know that,” she continued, “but what I do know is that they really did believe that, structurally, those things are what protect us against excesses in executive power.”

Sotomayor has continued to publicly rail against the 6-3 decision that granted Trump and former presidents presumptive criminal immunity for their official acts, recently saying she hopes the decision will ultimately be overturned.

On Friday, speaking at an American Philosophical Society event, Sotomayor again condemned the decision and said she doesn’t believe the remaining institutional controls in the political system are enough.

 “I think what they missed was the concept that there was no man in this country — and I use the male version, because that’s the saying — that no man was above the law here,” she said of her colleagues. “I think [that] was always something that was an important part of the calculus in which executives made their decision.”

Sotomayor notably didn’t shut down talk of Supreme Court term limits when asked by an audience member during the 45-minute discussion, though she said it was up to elected officials to decide. The justice noted other countries that don’t have judicial lifetime appointments.

“They either have age limits or they have term limits,” Sotomayor said. “So, they have not needed it to keep um politics out of influencing their judges in the way our founders worried. So, that’s something that should give you pause.”

data.title: Court formally approves $7.25B class settlement for cancer claims from Roundup weed killer
data.description:
A judge Friday formally approved a proposed $7.25 billion agreement to settle current and future cancer claims related to exposure of Monsanto’s Roundup weed killer.

The decision, by Missouri Judge Timothy Boyer, wraps up years of litigation in which people alleged that their exposure to Roundup caused them to develop blood cancers known as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The judge described the settlement as being “among the largest in history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.”

Monsanto and the plaintiffs suing it reached the settlement agreement in February and received preliminary approval in March.

After the agreement and preliminary approval, the Supreme Court made it more difficult for some similar cases to be heard in the future. It particularly ruled that people cannot sue pesticide companies for failing to warn of health impacts not formally recognized by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The EPA has not linked glyphosate, a key ingredient in Roundup, to health impacts like cancer. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer described it as “probably carcinogenic” to humans.

Boyer cited the Supreme Court’s decision in his final approval of the settlement agreement, saying that even without it, Monsanto has won a majority of related cases.

Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed lawyer for one of the subclasses in the case, praised the decision as helping people who were exposed to the weed killer.

“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” Seeger wrote in a statement. 

Meanwhile, Bill Anderson, the CEO of Bayer, which owns Monsanto, described the approval as “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” in a written statement. 

Pesticide issues, including those related to glyphosate, have also become a major cause of the Make America Healthy Again movement linked to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Trump administration backed Monsanto at the Supreme Court.

data.title: Casten, Lieu propose whistleblower program for prediction market insider trading
data.description:
Reps. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) and Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) introduced new legislation Friday to regulate prediction markets and prevent insider trading, allowing whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing.

The Policing Insider Trading in Prediction Markets Act would create a program at the Justice Department for people with knowledge of insider trading to come forward and potentially receive financial compensation for information leading to successful enforcement.

“Prediction markets have a serious insider trading problem,” Casten said. “By encouraging whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing, we can take an important step in cracking down on insider trading to restore accountability and public confidence in the U.S. rule of law.”

Improper use of betting markets has been in the spotlight multiple times this year, among political candidates, servicemembers and even White House staff.

In August, President Trump’s teleprompter operator was placed on leave and investigated for placing bets on the content of the president’s speeches before they were made public. Later that month, a Republican congressional candidate in North Carolina was suspended from Kalshi for betting on her own race. Kalshi had previously suspended three other congressional candidates in April.

Other examples of misuse include a U.S. Army soldier betting on the U.S. operation in Venezuela and nine accounts on Polymarket making $2.4 million on bets about military action in Iran. House Oversight Committee chair Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) announced an investigation into Kalshi and Polymarket in May.

In a statement about the bill Friday, Lieu cited some of the examples as a reason for legislative action.

“Government insiders should not be able to profit from betting on U.S. military operations or the contents of a President’s speech. They should not be able to use their positions of public trust to manipulate prediction markets,” Lieu said.

Kalshi recently said it had eliminated the option to place bets on Trump’s comments in response to a Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) order, having previously argued that Trump-mention markets “present a heightened risk of manipulation.”

With Republicans still in the majority, Casten and Lieu’s bill will need bipartisan support to pass before the end of the year, though it could be reintroduced once the new Congress — with a sizable Democratic majority — is sworn in.

data.title: Exclusive: Shaheen, Coons call for 'swift' response to Russian incursions into allied airspace
data.description:
Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.) and Chris Coons (Del.) condemned Russia for its recent reported incursions into the airspace of American allies, saying in a statement shared with The Hill Friday the U.S. should respond immediately.

“This dangerous pattern of hybrid attacks that Putin has unleashed on our partners, particularly NATO countries, is a test of our resolve and an effort to fracture our support for Ukraine,” the senators said.

Multiple U.S. allies reported Russian incursions into their airspace, with Japan and Taiwan both detecting Russian aircraft earlier this week. Poland said Friday multiple Russian “objects,” including a missile, had fallen into the country, and one had exploded. No injuries or damage were reported.

This is not the first time Russian aircraft have entered allied airspace this year; multiple fighter jets from Russia flew over Estonia, a NATO member, in September — a move which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called “unacceptable” at the time.

Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Coons went on to blast President Trump for his friendly posture toward Russian President Vladimir Putin during a trilateral meeting between the pair and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

While in Asia, Trump greeted Xi with an embrace on the tarmac and called Putin his “friend.” At a Friday press briefing, Trump said he had a good relationship with Putin and called it “very good” that Russia has a nuclear weapons stockpile.

“While President Trump gives Vladimir Putin a warm embrace, Russia continues its unacceptable incursions into the airspace of America’s allies,” Shaheen and Coons said. “This dangerous pattern of hybrid attacks that Putin has unleashed on our partners, particularly NATO countries, is a test of our resolve and an effort to fracture our support for Ukraine.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment on the letter.

Trump’s warm reception of Putin was widely criticized by Democrats and even some Republicans.

“I think his friend invaded a sovereign nation and is responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Thursday. “That’s not company I would keep.”

Trump defended his comments in Friday’s press conference, arguing the U.S. is better off because of his relationship with Xi and Putin.

“You’re very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries,” the president said.

Trump has received backlash from members of both parties for his friendly tone toward Russia in contrast to his sometimes harsh rhetoric about Ukraine and its president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

The president previously said Ukraine should replace Zelensky, and blamed high energy costs in the U.S. on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries instead of on the Iran war. Trump struck a deal with Russia this fall to purchase diesel from the country, a move which drew bipartisan backlash.

The president has repeatedly insisted he can bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end. His son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who is helping lead negotiations between the two countries, said Thursday Moscow is open to the idea of Kyiv having a mutual defense pact with Washington.

Russia, however, attacked Ukraine just hours after Trump and Putin’s meeting.

“Putin clearly left these meetings emboldened, not more willing to make peace,” Shaheen and Coons said. “Congress stands firm in our support for America’s allies, and we will maintain our commitment to defend America’s interests and support Ukraine against Russia’s unprovoked aggression.”

The Hill’s Laura Kelly contributed reporting.

The Big Story 

Trump shakes up cybersecurity leadership

The White House capped off a dramatic week of tech outages with a high-profile departure in its cybersecurity leadership. 

© Greg Nash

Sean Cairncross, the national cyber director, was let go from the role this week — the latest in a number of recent White House leadership shakeups.

 

President Trump backed the decision to let go of Cairncross because he didn’t think he had the cyber credentials for the job, a White House official told The Hill Thursday night.

 

The decision followed days of confusion and scrutiny about a wave of system outages that hit various sectors, including banks, tech companies and aviation. 

 

The Trump administration faced pressure to explain the reason behind these outages and, in the wake of such answers, conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and a so-called AI “doomsday” flooded the internet.

 

It’s not clear whether the White House’s response was what led to Carincross’s departure, but online users were quick to speculate on the timing. 

 

Cairncross sat at the top of the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), which manages cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. He previously served as chief of staff on National Security Council committees during Trump’s first term and then as an executive for the Millennium Challenge Corporation from 2019 to 2021. 

 

Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, is assuming the role in an acting capacity. The White House believes she has the credentials for the position, the official said. 

 

While ONCD has often managed to keep a lower profile in past presidencies, the advancements of AI have propelled cybersecurity concerns to the forefront over the past year as the tool becomes a potential weapon for adversaries and hackers. 

 

The now-former ONCD director reportedly clashed with other leaders of the president’s Cabinet on these issues. 

 

He allegedly believed the Treasury Department had become too involved with the team’s efforts, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his allies argued Cairncross had not been urgent with responding to questions about AI, according to Axios, which first reported on the departure.

 

And earlier today, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said he won’t allow Trump’s nominee for director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) to advance, leaving another gap in cyber leadership. 

 

Nick Anderson serves as CISA’s acting director.

 

The Hill’s Ryan Mancini has the full report on the shakeup.

data.title: Five takeaways from Trump's Friday news conference
data.description:
President Trump sought to regain momentum on Friday with a White House news conference that lasted almost 90 minutes.

Trump’s ostensible purpose was to talk up the achievements from his recent trip to Asia, which included the announcement of trade deals and, more controversially, a trilateral meeting with Chinese premier Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

On Friday, Trump was accompanied at the podium of the White House briefing room by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the presumptive frontrunners for the GOP’s 2028 presidential nomination if they enter the race.

But there was much more news than that. Here are five takeaways.

Trump strikes defensive tone over midterms defeat

The news conference came against the backdrop of the GOP’s big defeat in the midterm elections, in which Democrats easily took control of the House and flipped nine Senate seats for a comfortable majority in the upper chamber.

The results were widely seen as a rebuke to Trump, whose poll ratings have been languishing near all-time lows.

On Friday, Trump seemed in a rather sour mood about it.

“I wasn’t on the ballot, I hope you remember that,” he told the press corps at one point. Moments later, he insisted, “If I were on the ballot, it would have been a whole different story.”

There were odder moments, too.

At one stage, he appeared to insinuate that the price of oil had been artificially kept elevated through the midterm elections to hurt his party’s chances. 

It wasn’t clear whose hidden hand he felt was involved in this supposed sabotage. High gas prices have a far simpler explanation — the war on Iran, which Trump launched earlier this year.

While speaking about the midterms, Trump also claimed, “People thought that I was not treated well by the Republican Party because they didn’t get the things that I wanted passed.”

A fresh furor over Trump’s ‘friend’ Putin

One of the most controversial moments in Trump’s Asia trip came when he greeted Putin, saying, “He’s my friend.”

The president fueled the furor rather than tamping it down on Friday.

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins asked Trump if he believed Putin to be a friend “to America.”

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump replied. “I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia-Russia-Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it.”

The first five words of that response, seeming to dismiss the national interest, were a bad soundbite, at best, for Trump. Beyond that, his desire to once again re-litigate decade-old accusations of collusion between his 2016 campaign and Moscow has little salience to anyone outside of his MAGA base.

More broadly, Trump continues to characterize the war in Ukraine as driven by “serious animosity” between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. On Friday, he again seemed reluctant to focus on the actual cause of the war — Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Critics of Trump object more generally to his apparent admiration of authoritarian leaders. This was evident again at the press conference, beyond his comments on Putin, when he referred to Xi as “a great man”  who had “done a fantastic job for the country.”

It fell to Rubio to make a more strategic argument for these expressions of warmth. 

The secretary of State defended the trilateral meeting by saying that it would be “dangerous” if leaders like Trump, Xi and Putin were not able to engage with each other in a “conducive” environment.

Tensions linger with Vance over Iran

One of the more interesting analyses of the midterms came from the vice president, when he wrote in a lengthy social media post right afterwards that “the reason we lost is the war.”

This stark statement on the conflict in Iran was reported to have irked Trump, though the president has publicly denied annoyance.

Trump on Friday said that Vance’s statement was “fine — except I would have had one other thing that people were asking. I would have said that, would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

But, he insisted, there was “no problem there at all” with what Vance had said.

The issue is playing out against the backdrop of two other factors: Vance’s presumed 2028 ambitions, and the belief that he was more reluctant to back an attack on Iran than any other senior member of the administration.

Vance hardly put the chatter to rest when he was asked at the news conference whether he personally felt the war was worth losing control of the Senate. 

The vice president did not answer directly, instead citing the importance of keeping Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

He added: “The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again…My job is to support the President of the United States.”

The side-stepping of the core question — what is Vance’s personal view? — was glaring.

A hint of bipartisanship with Democrats

Trump has seemed to go back-and-forth since the midterms on whether he is inclined to try to work with Democrats or whether he will double down on a confrontational approach.

On Friday, he seemed more inclined toward the first approach — slightly.

The president did, to be sure, emphasize the power of the presidential veto. He said he was willing to use it repeatedly if Democrats passed legislation that he deemed unacceptable.

However, Trump also suggested that this approach could ultimately pave the way to more constructive discussions between him and Democrats in Congress.

He highlighted health care as one potential area of common ground, as well as the possibility of trying to boost the TV and movie production industry, and reforming college sports. 

Of course, Trump could revert to antagonism at a moment’s notice. But his comments for now seem to at least keep the door ajar to bipartisan legislation.

Another 2028 audition — with a Stephen Miller cameo

The visual effect of Vance and Rubio standing behind Trump on the podium was guaranteed to bring more speculation about each man’s electoral strength for 2028.

Each offered eager support for Trump when they spoke. Rubio addressed the room for longer than Vance, in part to defend the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting. The vice president spoke more briefly about trade deals and boosts to industry.

But the wildcard came when Stephen Miller, newly promoted to be White House chief of staff, was summoned to the lectern by Trump.

Miller is an enormously divisive figure, in part because of his hard-line approach to immigration and his extremely expansive view of presidential power.

Miller, speaking in his usual rapid-fire style, insisted that Trump had achieved more in the first two years of his second term than any other president “by far.” He further predicted that “the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history.”

This earned him a return in adulation from a happy president.

“He was better than these two guys,” Trump said, referring to Vance and Rubio. “Do you want to run for president?”

There is no realistic chance of Miller running to succeed Trump, but the admiring remark was a reminder of the chief-of-staff’s standing.

On the other hand, that had been clear even from the moment Trump introduced Miller on Friday. 

“We have the most powerful man in the world in the room right now,” Trump said. “Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.”

data.title: Senate GOP pushes through Trump judges in pre-holiday sprint
data.description:
Senate Republican leaders convened a rare Friday session to vote on a slate of President Trump’s judicial nominees. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has said he wants to confirm as many judges, who will serve for life, as possible before Democrats take power in January. 

“President Trump has more active judges on the appellate and district benches in this country than any other president,” Thune said in a floor speech earlier this week. “And that doesn’t happen by chance or happen by accident; it happens because we have been committed here in the United States Senate to ensuring that his judges move across the finish line at a fast pace.

After confirming two and teeing up final votes on five, the Senate left for Thanksgiving break. 

Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), the Republican whip, said in a speech Tuesday that confirming Trump’s judicial nominees is “the top priority” of Senate Republicans for the lame duck and repeated that Republicans “will leave no vacancy behind.”

He also praised the qualifications of the nominees and the judges confirmed so far and criticized Democrats for refusing to provide consent for judges to be easily confirmed during this Congress, slowing down the process.

“Democrats want to paralyze President Trump and derail anyone who challenges their liberal ideology,” Barrasso said.  “In the days and weeks ahead, Republicans will continue to burst through the Democrat blockade.”

Confirming nominees, including judges, is one of the Senate’s unique constitutional powers. But rules and procedures in the upper chamber also allow a single senator to hold up or block a judge nomination under some circumstances.

One judge won’t receive a vote anytime soon: T. Elliot Gaiser, Trump’s nominee for a district court in Texas, is currently awaiting a “blue slip,” or stamp of approval from outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). Cornyn is opposed to Gaiser because the latter is not from Texas and “has not been vetted.” 

But generally, Republicans have supported Trump’s nominees. 

Sen. Josh Hawley, who is on the Judiciary Committee, said he was glad the Senate had put so much emphasis on judges this Congress. He added that the Senate has confirmed Trump-appointed judges for all the vacancies in Missouri, which he said is significant for providing a Republican majority among the district judges in the state. 

“We want to get as many on the bench as possible,” said Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.). “I imagine we won’t get much opportunity here soon.”

data.title: Hinojosa outlines plans to end family detention at controversial ICE facility
data.description:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) shared her plan this week to end family detention at a controversial immigration detention center in the state in a conversation with YouTube children’s creator Ms. Rachel. 

“The reason we believe the children are being detained here with their families is because there’s licensing that allows that to happen,” Hinojosa said in a video shared Thursday on Instagram. “I would not allow that to happen. I would not ever license that — that’s child abuse. Should not be happening.”

The YouTube star, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, has taken a public stand to advocate against Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) practice of detaining families at Texas’s Dilley Immigration Processing Center. 

Earlier this month, Hinojosa told The New York Times she planned to use the state’s licensing power to prevent private prison companies from holding children in detention facilities in the state. Dilley is run by the private prison operator CoreCivic under contract with ICE. 

“Locking up little kids like that, even with their parents, that is child abuse,” Hinojosa told the outlet. 

Texas Rep. Joaquin Castro (D) responded to the Times article, saying he looked forward to working with the governor-elect to “shut down the Dilley Trailer Prison once and for all.”

“We must end family detention in America,” he wrote on social media. “No child should be ripped away from their lives and locked away. No private company should profit from the suffering and trauma of children.”

Castro visited the immigration processing center in January to meet with five-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos and his father, Adrian Conejo Arias, after they were detained and transported to the facility following their arrests in Minnesota. 

The Democratic representative announced the pair’s release and return to Minnesota on Feb. 1, and he has continued to advocate for the end of family detention practices. 

Hinojosa told Accurso that she was open to working with President Trump to “take care of kids and families.”

“Because we should be able to come together to stop hurting kids in this country and in this state,” she added. 

During a press conference on Friday, President Trump said he recently spoke with Hinojosa and that she was “really nice.”

“It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out,” he said. “Because that’s a very important thing. I got elected on the border, I did a phenomenal job.”

data.title: Trump asks Stephen Miller: 'Do you want to run for president?'
data.description:
President Trump floated his newly appointed chief of staff, longtime adviser Stephen Miller, as a potential presidential candidate — asking the top White House official if he was interested in the presidency during a press conference Friday afternoon.

The comment came after Miller heaped praise onto the president, with whom the chief of staff has worked since the start of Trump’s political career.

“No president has done what he has done over the last two years,” Miller said during the conference following the president’s visit to China earlier in the week, where he participated in rare trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history, and I’m so proud to be his chief of staff,” he added.

After Miller’s remarks, Trump joked with reporters in the briefing room, saying, “We have breaking news, he was better than these two guys” — referring to Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who both spoke earlier in the conference

“Do you want to run for president?” Trump then asked Miller.

Both Rubio and Vance have been floated among the GOP as possible presidential candidates for 2028, though neither have formally announced a bid. Vance told Fox News this week he would decide on running “sometime next year.” 

Though Rubio has reportedly said he’s not planning on a run next cycle, speculation surrounding his potential candidacy have continued to rise as Republicans look toward 2028 following a poor midterm performance.

Vance and Rubio also lauded the president during the press conference, congratulating him on striking trade deals with the Philippines and Thailand during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila earlier in the week.

Vance commended Trump’s work to “reorganize the global economy so that it makes sense to invest in the United States of America.”

Rubio also celebrated the president’s trilateral talks with Russia and China, which were divisive on both sides of the political aisle, pointing out that the three countries — despite being adversaries — collectively possess “the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet.”

“I am glad these leaders were able to engage,” Rubio said. “It set the tone and created a platform — created a foundation upon which hopefully, the hard work of diplomacy and trade negotiations can occur.”

data.title: Washington state finds Nippon Dynawave knew conditions were unsafe ahead of tank implosion
data.description:
Washington state fined Nippon Dynawave $10 million Friday, saying the company wilfully disregarded health and safety violations ahead of a chemical tank burst that killed 11 workers and injured a dozen others.

Washington’s labor and industries department said Friday that the penalty is the largest health and safety fine in state history.

“On May 26, 2026, the company’s inaction led to the worst industrial disaster in modern state history,” the department said in a release. “Dozens of violations related to that tank, other tanks on the site, the company’s emergency response, and the environmental impact have resulted in a combined $10,138,127 in penalties and cost recovery from state agencies.”

The Evergreen State said it would go a step further and refer Nippon to criminal authorities for investigation.

“Because Nippon’s safety and health violations were both willful and contributed directly to the deaths of their workers, L&I will also refer the case to the appropriate authorities for potential criminal prosecution,” the department said.

A representative for Nippon did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

A chemical tank holding white liquor, an ingredient for making paper, burst in May at Nippon’s paper mill in Longview, Wash., which the state called “the worst industrial disaster in modern state history.”

The state’s investigation, which interviewed more than 70 witnesses and reviewed tens of thousands of documents, found that the tank’s walls were thinner than the safe level and repair was mandated by state law. The department said that the Nippon received multiple reports of corroded walls that put the integrity of the tank at risk but did not act.

Joel Sacks, the director of the labor and industries department, called the state’s findings “shocking and heartbreaking” in a statement.

“Nippon Dynawave had all the information they needed to act, but they didn’t listen to alarms their consultants and staff were raising. Tragically, there are 11 families whose loved ones never came home as a result, and many others whose lives will be changed forever,” Sacks said.

After the disaster at Nippon and a near-disaster around the same time at a chemical plant in California, critics called for greater environmental regulation, especially at chemical sites. 

President Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had recently moved to roll back some regulations which impacted chemical plants, but the agency said the changes would not have impacted the incidents in Washington or California.
